transcript: I accidentally made cold calling easier by making the opener impossible to ignore. And you know what? Cold calling feels horrible. I'm terrible at it. But what we did is we sent the people we're calling a bottle of whiskey. So we sent this bottle of whiskey to adventure park owners. These are kind of eight-figure business owners, and we sent a letter with this bottle. And as you can see, the actual bottles of whiskey have a combination lock on the lid. Guess what? Around one-third of the business owners called us back. But not everyone. There was two-thirds of people that didn't, which means eventually I have to do the one thing I hate doing, which is picking up the phone and calling them. And I just ask if they've got it. And that used to feel awkward if I hadn't sent something beforehand. But now if I'm calling someone, I can just say, 'Listen, did you get that bottle of whiskey I sent you?' And then it naturally progresses to getting them on a call and closing them with our AI offer. And the reason it works so well is, yeah, I've spent £30, $40, whatever it is on this bottle of whiskey, but it's well worth it, especially because the type of people I'm calling are like own big businesses. And that's the power of direct mail. It makes the cold call much more warmer before you even speak, especially if they've got it, and we send it by tracked post. It gives you a reason to start conversation without feeling like a desperate salesperson. And sometimes the best outreach strategy is just doing something that makes people feel like they should respond.
